text: Two GitHub Actions jobs launch coding agents on self-hosted runners that mount the same repository checkout. explanation:
Objective 5.1 - Operate and manage multi-agent workflows

Concurrent coding agents need separate places to make and stage changes. A branch identifies a line of history, while a working tree contains the files and index used during editing. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/modules/multi-agent-systems-orchestration/4-execution-isolation-permissions-concurrency

D: This answer is incorrect because git worktree lock protects administrative state from pruning and the worktree from movement or deletion; it is not an editing lock between processes.

text: In Copilot CLI, what happens when a startup --allow-tool rule permits a tool operation whose underlying tool was excluded from the available tool set?
explanation:
Objective 2.1 - Select and configure agent tools

A runtime permission matters only when the agent has the relevant tool available. Copilot CLI separates the tools the model can choose from the permissions applied to their use. Excluding a tool removes it from that choice. An allow rule can reduce approval prompts for an available tool, but it cannot reverse that exclusion.

https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/allowing-tools

A timeout describes the missing result, not necessarily the state of the remote operation. Recovery should consider both the kind of failure and whether repeating the action could change the outcome twice. A side-effect-free read and a transient interruption support a limited retry. D: This answer is correct because retry safety depends on the operation's effects as well as the error. A write may have completed even when its response was lost.
E: This answer is incorrect because an invalid input remains invalid when the unchanged request is repeated. A retry policy for temporary connectivity does not correct a request-validation problem.
